Prompt: Explain code quality metrics such as cyclomatic complexity and code coverage.
ChatGPT Output: Code Quality Metrics Code quality metrics are measurements used to check how good, maintainable, reliable, and testable a software program is. Two important metrics are Cyclomatic Complexity and Code Coverage. 1. Cyclomatic Complexity Cyclomatic complexity measures the number of independent paths through a program. In simple words: It tells us how complicated the logic of the code is. The more if, else, for, while, case, etc. a program has, the higher its cyclomatic complexity can become. Example Javaif (age >= 18) { if (hasID) { System.out.println("Allowed"); } } There are two decision points: if (age >= 18) if (hasID) A commonly used formula is: Cyclomatic Complexity = Number of decision points + 1 So: CC = 2 + 1 = 3 This means there are 3 independent execution paths that should be considered during testing. Why is it useful? High cyclomatic complexity means: Code is harder to understand. More test cases are needed. Maintenance becomes harder. There is a greater chance of bugs. So developers generally try to keep complexity manageable by breaking large functions into smaller ones. 2. Code Coverage Code coverage measures how much of the code is executed by the test cases. In simple words: It tells us how much of our code has actually been tested. Example Suppose your program has 100 executable lines. Your test cases execute 80 of those lines. Then: Code Coverage = (Lines executed / Total executable lines) × 100 = (80 / 100) × 100 = 80% So the code has 80% line coverage. Types of Code Coverage 1. Line Coverage Checks how many lines of code were executed. 2. Statement Coverage Checks how many statements were executed. 3. Branch Coverage Checks whether different branches of conditions were tested. Example: Javaif (marks >= 40) System.out.println("Pass"); else System.out.println("Fail"); Good branch coverage would test both: marks >= 40 → Pass marks < 40 → Fail Cyclomatic Complexity vs Code Coverage MetricWhat it measuresCyclomatic ComplexityHow complicated the program's control flow isCode CoverageHow much of the program is executed during testingHigh value meansMore complexity → potentially harder to testHigh coverage meansMore code has been exercised by tests Easy way to remember 🧠 Cyclomatic Complexity → “How complicated is my code?” Code Coverage → “How much of my code did my tests touch?” And importantly, 100% code coverage does not guarantee bug-free software—the tests themselves may not check the right behavior.

Factory Pattern What is it? The Factory pattern creates objects without requiring the calling code to know the exact class being instantiated. Example Suppose we have different types of notifications: Notification ↓ ┌───────┬───────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ Email SMS Push Instead of writing: Javanew EmailNotification(); new SMSNotification(); throughout the application, we can use a factory. Prompt: Explain SOLID principles with short code examples.
ChatGPT Output: SOLID Principles SOLID is a set of 5 object-oriented design principles that help make software easy to understand, maintain, extend, and test. The five principles are: S — Single Responsibility Principle O — Open/Closed Principle L — Liskov Substitution Principle I — Interface Segregation Principle D — Dependency Inversion Principle 1. S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) A class should have only one responsibility. A class should have one main reason to change. ❌ Bad Javaclass Employee { void calculateSalary() { // calculate salary } void saveToDatabase() { // save employee } void generateReport() { // generate report } } This class is doing three different jobs. ✅ Better Javaclass SalaryCalculator { void calculateSalary() { // calculate salary } } class EmployeeRepository { void saveToDatabase() { // save employee } } class ReportGenerator { void generateReport() { // generate report } } Now each class has a single responsibility. 2. O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP) A class should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new functionality without repeatedly modifying existing code. ❌ Bad Javaclass Payment { void pay(String type) { if (type.equals("UPI")) { // UPI payment } else if (type.equals("Card")) { // Card payment } } } If we add PayPal, we have to modify the existing class. ✅ Better Javainterface Payment { void pay(); } class UPIPayment implements Payment { public void pay() { System.out.println("UPI payment"); } } class CardPayment implements Payment { public void pay() { System.out.println("Card payment"); } } Now we can add: Javaclass PayPalPayment implements Payment { public void pay() { System.out.println("PayPal payment"); } } without changing the existing payment classes. 3. L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) A child class should be usable wherever its parent class is expected without breaking the program. In simple words: A subclass should behave properly as a replacement for its parent. Example Suppose: Javaclass Bird { void fly() { System.out.println("Flying"); } } Now: Javaclass Penguin extends Bird { void fly() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } } This is a problem because penguins cannot fly. Code expecting a Bird may call fly() and fail. A better design would separate flying birds from non-flying birds: Javaclass Bird { void eat() { System.out.println("Eating"); } } interface FlyingBird { void fly(); } class Eagle extends Bird implements FlyingBird { public void fly() { System.out.println("Flying"); } } class Penguin extends Bird { // Doesn't need fly() } Now the classes behave appropriately. 4. I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) A class should not be forced to implement methods it does not need. Instead of creating one huge interface, create smaller, specific interfaces. ❌ Bad Javainterface Worker { void work(); void eat(); } Suppose a robot is a worker: Javaclass Robot implements Worker { public void work() { System.out.println("Working"); } public void eat() { // Robot doesn't eat! } } The robot is forced to implement an unnecessary method. ✅ Better Javainterface Workable { void work(); } interface Eatable { void eat(); } class Robot implements Workable { public void work() { System.out.println("Working"); } } class Human implements Workable, Eatable { public void work() { System.out.println("Working"); } public void eat() { System.out.println("Eating"); } } Now each class implements only what it needs. 5. D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) High-level classes should depend on abstractions, not directly on low-level classes. In simple words: Depend on an interface, not a specific implementation. ❌ Bad Javaclass EmailService { void sendEmail() { System.out.println("Email sent"); } } class Notification { EmailService email = new EmailService(); void notifyUser() { email.sendEmail(); } } Notification is tightly connected to EmailService. ✅ Better Javainterface MessageService { void send(); } class EmailService implements MessageService { public void send() { System.out.println("Email sent"); } } class Notification { private MessageService service; Notification(MessageService service) { this.service = service; } void notifyUser() { service.send(); } } Now we can use another service: Javaclass SMSService implements MessageService { public void send() { System.out.println("SMS sent"); } } The Notification class doesn't need to change. Quick Revision Table 🧠 LetterPrincipleSimple MeaningSSingle ResponsibilityOne class → One responsibilityOOpen/ClosedExtend without modifying existing codeLLiskov SubstitutionChild should properly replace parentIInterface SegregationDon't force unnecessary methodsDDependency InversionDepend on abstractions/interfaces Easy memory trick S → Single job O → Open to extension L → Let child replace parent I → Interfaces should be small D → Depend on interfaces Together, SOLID principles help produce code that is more maintainable, flexible, reusable, and easier to test.

Accounting Method Imagine every cheap operation pays a little extra. For example: Normal insertion cost = 1 Extra saved amount = 1 That extra amount helps pay for future resizing. So cheap operations effectively save credits that are later used for expensive operations. 3. Potential Method Assign a potential value to the data structure. When the array has unused capacity, it has stored potential that can help pay for a future resize. This is a more mathematical version of the accounting idea. 🧠 Easy Analogy Imagine a person saving money: Every month: Save ₹100 Occasionally, they have a big expense: Laptop repair → ₹500 One month has a large expense, but because money was saved during previous months, the average cost over many months remains manageable. Paging is a memory-management technique that divides memory into fixed-size blocks. Example Suppose a process is divided into pages: Process +-------+-------+-------+-------+ | Page 0| Page 1| Page 2| Page 3| +-------+-------+-------+-------+ Physical RAM is divided into frames: RAM +--------+--------+--------+--------+ | Frame 0| Frame 1| Frame 2| Frame 3| +--------+--------+--------+--------+ The pages don't have to be stored next to each other. For example: Page 0 → Frame 2 Page 1 → Frame 0 Page 2 → Frame 3 Page 3 → Frame 1 The OS maintains a page table to keep track of this mapping. Page Table Page Frame ---- ----- 0 → 2 1 → 0 2 → 3 3 → 1 Why is paging useful? It allows a process to use memory without requiring one large continuous block of physical RAM. It also helps avoid external fragmentation. 2. What is Virtual Memory? Virtual memory allows a process to use an address space that can be larger than the available physical RAM. The OS uses secondary storage, such as an SSD/HDD, as a backing store when needed. Example Suppose: Process size = 8 GB RAM available for it = 4 GB The entire 8 GB does not need to be in RAM simultaneously. Some pages can remain on disk: Process 8 GB virtual | +--------+--------+ | | RAM Disk 4 GB backing store When the CPU needs a page that isn't currently in RAM, a page fault occurs. 3. What is a Page Fault? Suppose the CPU wants Page 5. The page table says: Page 5 → Not currently in RAM This causes a page fault. The OS then: Finds the required page on disk. Finds a free frame in RAM. Loads the page into that frame. Updates the page table. Restarts/continues the interrupted instruction. If there is no free frame, the OS must choose an existing page to remove. This is where page replacement algorithms are used. 4. Page Replacement Suppose RAM has only 3 frames: Frame 1 Frame 2 Frame 3 They are already full: +-------+-------+-------+ | 2 | 5 | 1 | +-------+-------+-------+ Now the CPU requests page 7. Before: 1 | 2 | 3 After: 1 | 4 | 3 So Page 2 is replaced by Page 4. Prompt: Explain deadlock and the four necessary conditions with a resource allocation example.
ChatGPT Output: Deadlock in Operating Systems A deadlock is a situation where two or more processes are waiting for each other indefinitely, so none of them can continue. Simple real-life example 🚗 Imagine two cars on a narrow road: Car A → needs the space occupied by Car B Car B → needs the space occupied by Car A Both are waiting, so neither can move. That is similar to a deadlock in an operating system. Resource Allocation Example Suppose we have: Two processes: P1 and P2 Two resources: R1 and R2 Each resource has one instance. Initially: R1 → P1 R2 → P2 So: P1 is holding R1 and needs R2. P2 is holding R2 and needs R1. holds holds P1 ─────────→ R1 R2 ←───────── P2 | | | needs | needs ↓ ↓ R2 R1 Now: P1 waits for R2 P2 waits for R1 Neither can proceed. Therefore: P1 waits for P2 → P2 waits for P1 → DEADLOCK Four Necessary Conditions for Deadlock A deadlock can occur only when all four conditions exist at the same time. These are also called the Coffman conditions. 1. Mutual Exclusion A resource can be used by only one process at a time. For example: Printer → P1 P2 cannot use the printer until P1 releases it. P1 ────→ Printer P2 ────→ Printer ❌ So the resource is mutually exclusive. 2. Hold and Wait A process is holding one resource while waiting for another resource. In our example: P1 holds R1 P1 waits for R2 At the same time: P2 holds R2 P2 waits for R1 So both processes are holding something and waiting for something else. 3. No Preemption A resource cannot be forcibly taken away from a process. The process must voluntarily release the resource after it finishes using it. For example: P1 holds R1 The OS cannot simply take R1 from P1 and give it to P2. P1 must release R1 itself. 4. Circular Wait There must be a circular chain of processes waiting for each other. Our example: P1 waits for R2 ↓ held by ↓ P2 ↓ P2 waits for R1 ↓ held by ↓ P1 This creates a circle: P1 → P2 → P1 Therefore, circular wait exists. Complete Resource Allocation Graph We can represent the situation as: holds P1 ─────────→ R1 ↑ | | | | needs | | ↓ R2 ←───────── P2 holds More clearly: holds P1 ─────────→ R1 │ ↑ │ │ needs │ P2 │ │ needs ↓ R2 ←───────── P2 holds The important idea is: P1 holds R1 → waits for R2 P2 holds R2 → waits for R1 So: P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1 There is a cycle, indicating deadlock when each resource has a single instance. Why Are All Four Conditions Necessary? ConditionMeaning in our exampleMutual ExclusionR1/R2 can be held by only one processHold and WaitP1 holds R1 while waiting for R2No PreemptionR1/R2 cannot be forcibly takenCircular WaitP1 waits for P2 and P2 waits for P1 If even one of these four conditions is prevented, the deadlock can be prevented. For example, if you installed: Windows + Ubuntu you may normally see: GRUB Menu ---------------- Ubuntu Advanced options for Ubuntu Windows Boot Manager ---------------- If GRUB is damaged or incorrectly configured, you might see errors such as: grub rescue> or the computer may boot directly into only one operating system. 1. First Check the Boot Mode Before repairing GRUB, determine whether your system uses: UEFI Legacy BIOS On Ubuntu, you can check with: Bash[ -d /sys/firmware/efi ] && echo "UEFI" || echo "Legacy BIOS" If it prints: UEFI your system is using UEFI. If you can enter Ubuntu, first update GRUB: Bashsudo update-grub You may see: Found Windows Boot Manager Found Ubuntu Then reboot: Bashsudo reboot The GRUB menu should now contain the detected operating systems. 3. If Ubuntu Boots but Windows Is Missing This is a common dual-boot problem. Run: Bashsudo update-grub If Windows is still not detected, check whether os-prober is installed: Bashsudo apt install os-prober Then enable it if your Ubuntu version/configuration requires it: Bashsudo nano /etc/default/grub Add or uncomment: GRUB_DISABLE_OS_PROBER=false Save the file and run: Bashsudo update-grub Then reboot: Bashsudo reboot 4. If GRUB Is Completely Broken If Ubuntu itself doesn't boot, you can use an Ubuntu Live USB. Step 1: Boot from the Ubuntu USB Choose: Try Ubuntu instead of installing Ubuntu. 5. Your system will have its own layout. 6. Mount the Ubuntu Partition Suppose your Ubuntu partition is /dev/nvme0n1p3. Mount it: Bashsudo mount /dev/nvme0n1p3 /mnt For a UEFI installation, also mount the EFI System Partition. Suppose it is /dev/nvme0n1p1: Bashsudo mount /dev/nvme0n1p1 /mnt/boot/efi Again, the partition names must match your lsblk -f output. 7. Reinstall GRUB For a UEFI system, after mounting the Ubuntu and EFI partitions, you can reinstall GRUB into the mounted system: Bashsudo grub-install \ --boot-directory=/mnt/boot \ --efi-directory=/mnt/boot/efi \ /dev/nvme0n1 Then regenerate the GRUB configuration: Bashsudo chroot /mnt update-grub exit Finally: Bashsudo reboot Remove the USB when the computer restarts. Important: GRUB repair commands depend on whether the machine uses UEFI or Legacy BIOS and on your partition layout. Don't substitute /dev/nvme0n1p1, /dev/nvme0n1p3, etc. without checking your own system. 8. Using Boot-Repair Another option is Boot-Repair, a graphical tool commonly used for fixing bootloader problems. You can boot an Ubuntu Live USB and use Boot-Repair to diagnose and repair common GRUB problems. It can be useful when you aren't comfortable identifying partitions manually. Problem 2: Ubuntu boots but Windows isn't shown Try: Bashsudo update-grub and, if necessary, configure os-prober as described above. Problem 3: grub rescue> appears This generally means GRUB cannot find its configuration or required files. A common solution is to boot an Ubuntu Live USB and repair/reinstall GRUB. If Ubuntu still boots, sudo update-grub can regenerate its menu. If it does not boot, an Ubuntu Live USB can be used to identify and mount the Ubuntu and EFI partitions and reinstall/regenerate GRUB.

Docker Volumes A Docker volume is a storage area managed by Docker that exists separately from the container. Why use it? Container data normally disappears when the container is deleted. A volume keeps the data persistent. Multiple containers can potentially share a volume. Example: Container → Volume → Data Even if the container is removed, the data in the volume remains. 2. Docker Networks A Docker network allows containers to communicate with each other. For example: Flask Container ───────→ MySQL Container │ │ └──── Docker Network ───┘ The Flask application can communicate with MySQL using the service name db instead of an IP address. Multi-container Example with Docker Compose Suppose we have: Flask → web application MySQL → database Volume → stores MySQL data Network → connects Flask and MySQL compose.yaml YAMLservices: web: build: . ports: - "5000:5000" depends_on: - db networks: - app-network db: image: mysql:8.0 environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root MYSQL_DATABASE: mydb volumes: - db-data:/var/lib/mysql networks: - app-network volumes: db-data: networks: app-network: How it works Docker Compose │ ┌──────────┴──────────┐ ↓ ↓ Flask Container MySQL Container │ │ └──── app-network ────┘ │ ↓ db-data volume Important parts web service: YAMLports: - "5000:5000" Maps host port 5000 → container port 5000. depends_on: YAMLdepends_on: - db Tells Compose to start the db service before the web service. Network: YAMLnetworks: - app-network Both containers join the same network and can communicate. For example, Flask can connect to MySQL using: host = db not localhost. The three important practices are IAM, encryption, and least privilege. 1. IAM — Identity and Access Management IAM controls who can access cloud resources and what they are allowed to do. For example, an organization may have: Admin → Full access Developer → Application access Intern → Limited access IAM typically involves: Authentication → Who are you? Authorization → What are you allowed to access? Roles and policies → What permissions are assigned? Example In AWS, an IAM policy might allow a developer to read objects from a storage bucket but not delete them. IAM = Managing identities and permissions. 2. Encryption Encryption converts readable data into an unreadable form so unauthorized users cannot easily access it. There are two important types: Data at rest Protects stored data such as: Database records Cloud storage Backups Original data ↓ Encryption ↓ Encrypted data Data in transit Protects data while it is moving between systems, commonly using TLS/HTTPS. User ──── encrypted connection ────→ Cloud server Encryption = Protecting data from unauthorized reading. 3. Least Privilege The principle of least privilege means giving a user, application, or service only the permissions it needs to perform its task—and no unnecessary permissions. Example Suppose an application only needs to read files from a storage bucket. Instead of: Read + Write + Delete + Admin give it: Read only This reduces the damage if the account or application is compromised. Least privilege = Minimum required permissions. Other Common Cloud Security Practices Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) Requires more than one method of authentication. Password + OTP Even if a password is stolen, the attacker may still be unable to log in. Security Monitoring Monitor: Login attempts API calls Configuration changes Suspicious activity Cloud platforms provide logging and monitoring services to detect unusual behavior. Regular Backups Maintain backups so data can be recovered after accidental deletion, system failure, or ransomware. Network Security Use: Firewalls/security groups Private networks Network segmentation Restricted inbound/outbound traffic Quick Revision PracticePurposeIAMControls identities and accessEncryptionProtects dataLeast PrivilegeGives only necessary permissionsMFAStrengthens authenticationMonitoringDetects suspicious activityBackupsEnables data recoveryNetwork SecurityControls network traffic Easy way to remember IAM → Who can access? Least privilege → What can they access? Encryption → Can unauthorized people read the data?

The goal is: Find the minimum number of vertices that cover all edges. This is called the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. Why Approximation? Finding the minimum vertex cover exactly is computationally expensive for large graphs. So we can use a simple approximation algorithm. 2-Approximation Algorithm The standard algorithm works like this: Step 1 Choose any uncovered edge (u,v). Step 2 Add both u and v to the vertex cover. Step 3 Remove/mark all edges covered by u or v. Step 4 Repeat until no edges remain. Example Consider: A ----- B | | | | C ----- D Start with edge: (A,B) Add both: {A,B} Now all edges touching A or B are covered. The remaining edge is: (C,D) Add C and D: {A,B,C,D} So the approximation algorithm gives: C={A,B,C,D} However, the optimal solution for this particular graph is: {A,D} with only 2 vertices. So this example shows that the approximation algorithm doesn't necessarily find the minimum solution. Why is it called a 2-Approximation? The important guarantee is: ∣C∣≤2∣C∗∣​ where: C = solution produced by approximation algorithm C∗ = optimal minimum vertex cover So the algorithm produces a solution that is at most twice the optimal size. It doesn't mean the answer will always be exactly twice as large. It could be equal to the optimum or somewhere between the optimum and twice the optimum. Why does the guarantee work? Suppose the algorithm chooses these edges: (u1​,v1​),(u2​,v2​),…,(uk​,vk​) These selected edges cannot share vertices, because after selecting an edge, all edges touching its endpoints are removed. Therefore, they form a matching. Any valid vertex cover must contain at least one endpoint from each of these k edges. So: ∣C∗∣≥k Our algorithm selects both endpoints of each edge: ∣C∣=2k Therefore: ∣C∣=2k≤2∣C∗∣ Hence it is a 2-approximation algorithm.
